# Fantasy and the Thought Life

> "but I tell you that everyone who gazes at a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart."
>
> — Matthew 5:28

Lust starts in the eyes and the mind, long before it reaches a website or a hand. So this chapter is about the look and the thought.

Start with a man from the last chapter, whose case is sly enough to need a closer look. He has quit porn, and he means it. He hasn't opened one of those sites in months. He has a red line and he stays on the right side of it.

On the right side of it are Instagram, TikTok, YouTube and Twitch. There are the fitness models, the "try-on hauls", and the beach photos of a girl he was at school with. None of it would trip a filter. And when the phone is in another room there's the reel in his own head. It holds old girlfriends, scenes he watched years ago, and the woman from the gym.

You know how the evening goes. Your wife is tired, or you have no wife, and you feel you're owed something. "I won't look at porn. I'll just scroll for a bit." Forty minutes later you're in the bathroom. Or you don't finish at all, and you go to bed pleased with yourself and wide awake.

Two things make this worse than it looks. First, it props up the belief that you're being deprived. Every swipe tells you that the real feast is over the line and you're a good boy for eating crumbs on the doorstep. Second, it eats your self-respect. An honest man finds himself tilting his screen away from his wife.

## Crumbs are still a meal {-}

The Little Monster doesn't care where his food comes from. Scraps keep him alive as well as a banquet does. The "soft" stuff in your feed gives the itch a moment's ease, which is all it needs to stay awake until next time.

One coach is blunt about what a man is doing when he feeds on pictures of women he'll never meet: "you're settling for the consolation prize". And the feed learns. Pause on one photo for two seconds and it brings you ten more tomorrow. It's a machine for finding your red line and parking you next to it.

The same coach's picture of the man with the phone is not a kind one: "satisfying yourself to her pixels like a loser". And what is that man to the woman in the photograph? "you're just another like on her photo".

Sometimes he is less than a like. Plenty of the women in that feed are running a business, and the product is your thirst. The coach describes the deal from her side of the screen: "she got the leverage". Solomon warned his son about the same trade: "lest strangers feast on your wealth, and your labors enrich another man's house." You met the lever in Chapter 8. The feed is where it gets pulled.

The woman on the screen is beautiful. Nobody is denying it. If she were your wife, and in the room, she'd be a gift. But she isn't in the room. She's light on a piece of glass. A trout that rises to a feathered hook doesn't get fed either.

A boiler has a pilot light, a tiny flame that burns all day and uses almost no gas. Its only job is to make sure the main burner can fire the instant it's asked. That's what the scroll and the daydream are. You never do it "out of nowhere". The pilot light has been on since breakfast.

## "Then I'll look and not touch" {-}

Read the verse that opens this chapter again. Jesus doesn't draw the line at the hand, or at a certain kind of website. He draws it at the gaze.

Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say that seeing a beautiful woman is a sin, or that a thought arriving is a sin. A veteran of the recovery forums put the distinction well: "Admiration of beauty is not lust, know the difference." The difference is in three small words: "to lust after". That's a look with a purpose. It's the second look, the lingering one, the one you go back for. You always know which kind you're doing. The scroll is a purposeful gaze pretending to be an accident.

A well-known pastor tells a story against himself. Nearly thirty years ago he was flicking through the channels and landed on women in bikinis. He hesitated for about two seconds, and his wife saw. She asked him one question: "Well, was it worth it?" He has been repeating his answer from the pulpit ever since: a moment of lust is never worth it.

It took two seconds, and he never touched anything. Under one man's testimony a commenter explained why it matters anyway: "Lustful thoughts are just as addictive and as awful as the act".

## The harem in your head {-}

No filter blocks a memory. That's why some men think the reel is the safe option.

C.S. Lewis didn't. In 1956 a man wrote to him about masturbation, and you've already met his answer: the prison of himself, and the harem of imaginary brides. Here is where he took it. The imaginary women are always available. They never refuse, and they never ask a man to give anything up. So, Lewis wrote, "this harem, once admitted, works against his ever getting out and really uniting with a real woman." A real woman has moods, needs and a mind of her own. The harem has none, so she's the one who starts to feel like hard work.

Then comes his warning: "The danger is that of coming to love the prison."

That's the cost of the thought life. Each time, the cell gets a little more comfortable.

## The woman in the room {-}

The feed and the reel are made of women who aren't there. The same eye works on the ones who are.

You know the second look at the woman in the next aisle. You know the conversation at work that runs a little longer than it needs to, and why. You know the small glow when she laughs at your joke, and how much of your afternoon then goes on earning another one. None of it would count as doing anything. All of it is the Little Monster eating.

Paul gave a young pastor a rule for this that is hard to improve on. Treat "the elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, in all purity." A man doesn't size up his sister, or perform for her, or keep a door open with her. He's simply glad she's there. That is how a free man gets to treat every woman he meets, and the women can tell the difference at once.

## Taking thoughts captive {-}

Paul describes a different way to live: "bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:5).

That doesn't mean "try not to think about it". You've tried that, and you know it turns the thought into the biggest thing in the room. A captive is a thought that has been stopped at the gate and asked what it wants. There's an old saying that you can't stop a bird flying over your head, but you can stop it building a nest in your hair. The first look is the bird. The reel is the nest.

That same pastor lays out the road from the bird to the nest in four steps: a thought, then imagination, then justification, then the choice. Notice how late the choice comes. By the time a man thinks he's deciding, three steps are behind him. A man on a recovery forum, who had read EasyPeasy, found the right place to stand: "The easiest thought for me to say, 'No' to, is the first one. And if I don't entertain the thought, I'm not going to do it."

It's also far easier than you fear. A man replays the reel for one reason: he believes there's something in it for him. Once he sees there isn't, the thought turns up, finds nobody home, and leaves. The coach from earlier starts his own advice in the same place: "the first thing you must do to desexualize your brain is to stop fantasizing about women you don't know". (You're still carrying on as normal until the end of the book. For now, just watch.)

If you're not a believer, call it noticing your thoughts before they notice you.

And here is what waits on the other side. A man on the NoFap forum, a hundred days out, noticed that the women around him had changed. Of course it was his eyes that had changed: "I stopped looking at girl's boobs/butts/legs and started noticing much more interesting things about them. Smiles, gestures". He was seeing people again.

Meanwhile our man stays at his red line with a phone full of crumbs.

AND HE CALLS IT BEING FREE!
